summary: Describes version 2.0 of a protocol IBM used in many of its SNMP agents so that the set of managed objects can be extended dynamically. It is an experimental protocol, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A control panel with fixed buttons can be hard to change. This is a way to plug in new buttons later without rebuilding the panel.

questions: how does snmp dpi register a mib sub-tree
how does snmp dpi handle set requests
subtitle: A lightweight protocol that lets separate sub-agent processes plug new MIB variables into a running SNMP agent.

tldr.problem: Conventional SNMP agents gave end users no way to add new management variables, and implementing many MIBs meant building one big monolithic agent.
tldr.mechanism: A sub-agent opens a connection to the agent over TCP, UDP or another transport, registers a MIB sub-tree, and then answers GET, GETNEXT, GETBULK and SET requests that the agent passes down as DPI packets.
tldr.outcome: This is version 2.0 of IBM's SNMP-DPI, offered as an Experimental protocol that obsoletes RFC 1228. It is not a standard, and the authors only say they may seek the standards track later.

today: RFC 1592 is an Experimental memo from March 1994. It obsoletes RFC 1228 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why Sub-agents
sections.content:
The Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) lets a manager read and set variables in a Management Information Base (MIB). An enterprise can define variables of its own, such as CPU utilization, but conventional agents offered no way for an end user to make them available. Without sub-agents, all MIBs must also live in one monolithic agent.

The Distributed Protocol Interface (DPI) lets a separate process register a variable or MIB sub-tree with the agent. The agent hands matching requests to that sub-agent and packages the answer as an ordinary SNMP response. Remote management stations cannot tell that other processes are involved. DPI also spares the sub-agent author from the details of ASN.1 and SNMP PDU encoding.

The RFC describes a protocol IBM implemented in most of its SNMP agents; versions 1.0 and 1.1 had been used within IBM since 1989 and version 1.2 within Bell Northern Research since 1992. The authors offer version 2.0 as experimental and invite feedback. They explicitly drop the programming API from this document, specifying only the agent-to-sub-agent protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of one giant program that knows everything, small helper programs each look after their own part, and the main program passes questions to the right helper.

sections.title: How a Sub-agent Connects and Works
sections.content:
The transport can be a stream such as TCP, or datagrams such as UDP; the VM agent also allows connections over IUCV. UDP exists because TCP sockets use up file descriptors on Unix. There is no well-known port: the agent listens on an arbitrary port that can differ on each run. The sub-agent learns it by sending one ordinary SNMP GET to UDP port 161 for dpiPortForTCP.0 (1.3.6.1.4.1.2.2.1.1.1.0) or dpiPortForUDP.0 (1.3.6.1.4.1.2.2.1.1.2.0).

Then the sub-agent sends OPEN to identify itself, with a timeout, the maximum varBinds per packet, a character set choice and an optional password. Next it sends REGISTER for each MIB sub-tree, with a requested priority and timeout. The agent answers both with a RESPONSE. After that the sub-agent waits for requests, or sends TRAP packets, which the agent forwards as SNMP traps. To stop, it sends UNREGISTER and CLOSE. A CLOSE gets no response and implicitly unregisters everything on that connection.

Either side can also send UNREGISTER or CLOSE. A sub-agent on an unreliable transport can send ARE_YOU_THERE to check that the agent still knows about it.
sections.plainLanguage: A helper first finds the front desk, introduces itself, says which questions it can answer, and then waits. When it is done for the day it says goodbye.

sections.title: DPI Packets and Codes
sections.content:
Every packet starts with a two-byte length of the data that follows, in network byte order, then the protocol major version, minor version and release, a 16-bit packet ID and a packet type. The packet ID is a monotonically increasing unsigned 16-bit integer that wraps, and lets each side match RESPONSEs to requests, which matters when UDP can lose packets.

Packet types run from 1 to 15 (GET is 1, RESPONSE is 5, OPEN is 8, ARE_YOU_THERE is 15); TRAPV2 (13) and INFORM (14) are marked not yet used. RESPONSE error codes use SNMPv2 style values 0 to 18 for GET, GETNEXT, GETBULK, SET, COMMIT and UNDO, and DPI-specific values 101 to 111 for OPEN, REGISTER and UNREGISTER, such as alreadyRegistered (103) and higherPriorityRegistered (104). Integers are 4 bytes in network byte order, and strings, including object identifiers, are in either the native or the ASCII character set that the sub-agent selects in OPEN.

Compared with the earlier RFC 1228, version 2.0 adds OPEN, CLOSE, ARE_YOU_THERE, UNREGISTER, COMMIT and UNDO packets, allows several varBinds per packet, and adds the packet ID and SNMPv2 error codes and value types.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message starts with a little label saying how long it is, what number it has and what kind of message it is, so the answer can be matched to the right question.

sections.title: Request Processing and Two-Phase SET
sections.content:
For a GET, the sub-agent returns the values for each varBind, or a NULL value of type noSuchObject or noSuchInstance, which are not errors. GETBULK is turned into multiple GETNEXT requests by default, unless the sub-agent asks in REGISTER to receive it.

A SET uses a two-phase commit so that all varBinds in one SNMP SET change "as if simultaneous". The agent sends SET, and the sub-agent only prepares (for instance, allocates resources). When every SET has succeeded, the agent sends COMMIT, and the sub-agent makes the change. If any SET fails, the agent sends UNDO to those that succeeded. If a COMMIT fails elsewhere, an UNDO can arrive even after a sub-agent committed, and it must try to reverse the change. Errors are commitFailed and undoFailed, which the text says should not be returned lightly.

The sub-agent must answer within the timeout. If it does not, the agent will most probably close the connection and discard a late RESPONSE.
sections.plainLanguage: When several changes must happen together, the boss first asks every helper if it is ready. Only when all say yes does the boss say go; if one says no, everyone cancels.

sections.title: Status and Security
sections.content: The memo defines an Experimental protocol and not an Internet standard. It notes that at a March 1992 IETF BOF there was not enough support to define a standard for multiplexing SNMP agents, and that SMUX had been changed to a historic RFC. The security section says only that security issues are not discussed in the memo, although OPEN can carry an optional password that the agent may use to validate a sub-agent.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a trial idea the authors want people to try out. The memo does not discuss security, apart from an optional password when connecting.

viz.caption: SUB-AGENT LIFECYCLE, SUMMARIZED FROM THE RFC

messages.label: OPEN
messages.note: Identifies itself, timeout, max varBinds, character set.

messages.label: REGISTER
messages.note: Registers a MIB sub-tree with a priority.

messages.label: GET / GETNEXT / SET
messages.note: Passed down from a manager's SNMP request.

messages.label: CLOSE
messages.note: No response; implies UNREGISTER of everything.

fields.name: Packet length
fields.desc: Length of the data to follow, MSB first.

fields.name: Packet ID
fields.desc: Matches responses to requests; wraps at its maximum.

fields.name: Packet type
fields.desc: OPEN, REGISTER, GET, SET and so on.

items.label: SNMP_DPI_GETNEXT
items.desc: Agent asks for the next variables.

items.label: SNMP_DPI_TRAP
items.desc: Sub-agent asks the agent to send a trap.

items.label: SNMP_DPI_COMMIT
items.desc: Make a prepared set take effect.

items.label: SNMP_DPI_GETBULK
items.desc: Bulk retrieval, if requested at registration.

items.label: SNMP_DPI_ARE_YOU_THERE
items.desc: Check the agent still knows the sub-agent.
